statement: Modern scholarship explicitly argues that a Near Eastern version of the divine-succession myth preserved in the Hurro-Hittite Song of Emergence was transmitted through eastern Mediterranean intercultural contact and adapted in Hesiod's Theogony.

sources.citation: Amir Gilan, “Let Those Important Primeval Deities Listen: The Social Setting of the Hurro-Hittite Song of Emergence,” in Gods and Mortals in Early Greek and Near Eastern Mythology (Cambridge University Press, 2021), pp. 19–36.
sources.author: Amir Gilan
sources.access_note: Cambridge summary calls this the clearest evidence for Greek reception of Near Eastern mythology and proposes performance near Mount Hazzi as a plausible transfer context.

sources.citation: Kostas Vlassopoulos, “The Barbarian repertoire in Greek culture,” in Greeks and Barbarians (Cambridge University Press, 2013), pp. 161–225.
sources.author: Kostas Vlassopoulos
sources.access_note: The chapter explicitly states that a version of the myth was transmitted through intercultural communication and adapted in Hesiod's Theogony.

sources.citation: Ian Rutherford, Hittite Texts and Greek Religion: Contact, Interaction, and Comparison (Oxford University Press, 2020), ch. 7, “Generations of Gods and the South-East.”
sources.author: Ian Rutherford
sources.access_note: Oxford abstract identifies the north-east Mediterranean/Levant-Cilicia zone as the most likely route if the Kingship in Heaven myths reached Greece.

does_not_demonstrate: The exact human transmitter, single route, and date of transmission are not known.
The evidence does not establish direct line-by-line textual copying from one surviving Hittite manuscript.
adversarial_counter: The route and mechanism remain partly reconstructive, and isolated motifs can be independently generated; the stronger case rests on the clustered succession pattern plus documented eastern Mediterranean contact.
notes: Backs a CULTURAL_FUSION edge rather than a claim of direct textual copying.
